extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, and applicants (patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and weighing applicant rebuttal arguments and evidence offered to overcome a prima facie obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 (including examples of acceptable evidence, procedural forms, and evidentiary standards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art method-of-making relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence or absence of a prior art suggestion of a method of making a claimed compound may be relevant in determining prima facie obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making a claimed compound at the relevant time, it may not be legally concluded that the compound itself is in the possession of the public; absence of a known or obvious process for making the claimed compounds overcomes a presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity. See In re Maloney; In re Hoeksema; In re Payne. Examiners should consider whether prior art methods would have provided those skilled in the art a means to make the claimed compound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation-of-similar-properties rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: A presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity may be overcome where there is evidence showing there is no reasonable expectation of similar properties in structurally similar compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant evidence establishing unpredictability in the pertinent art (e.g., showing structurally similar compounds do not share properties) can rebut a prima facie case. See In re May; In re Schechter; Ex parte Blattner. Examiner should consider such evidence when assessing obviousness based on structural analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art utility or intermediate-status
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior art compounds have no specific or significant utility, or are disclosed only as intermediates, structurally similar claimed compounds may not be prima facie obvious over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reference compounds lack meaningful utility or are merely synthetic intermediates, one of ordinary skill would not have reason to make or investigate related compounds; see In re Stemniski, In re Albrecht, In re Lalu. Examiners should assess whether the prior art provides a motivation to make the claimed compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results as rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected results must be supported by objective evidence (not mere argument or speculation). Comparative data, declarations, or experimental results that demonstrate an unexpected property or large improvement over prior art can rebut obviousness (e.g., In re Papesch; In re Wiechert). Unsupported assertions (e.g., unsupported expert testimony of unusually low immune response) are insufficient (In re Mayne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) as rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, copying, and other objective indicia of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence is part of the whole obviousness analysis and must be considered (see Graham; Piasecki; Soni; Leo Pharma). It can include evidence that the claimed invention was copied, market acceptance, licensing behavior, or expert opinions about the state of the art. However, secondary considerations do not automatically control the conclusion and must be weighed against the prima facie showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus and commensurateness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be accorded substantial weight, objective evidence of nonobviousness must have a nexus to the claimed invention and be commensurate in scope with the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant bears the burden of establishing nexus; a presumption of nexus requires the product embody the invention and be coextensive with the claims (Volvo Penta; Fox Factory v. SRAM). Evidence not commensurate in scope or relating to products not covered by the claims is not probative (GPAC; Paulsen; Kulling; Grasselli). MPEP §716.01(b) provides further nexus guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant burden and permissible forms of rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a prima facie case is made, the burden shifts to the applicant to come forward with arguments and/or evidence to rebut the prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may be presented in the specification, by affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.130/1.131/1.132, or otherwise during prosecution. Arguments cannot substitute for factually supported objective evidence (In re Soni; In re Schulze; In re De Blauwe). Guidance on which CFR provision applies is provided in MPEP §§ 715-716 and 2136.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner duty to consider and weigh all evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal arguments and evidence presented by applicants and weigh the proffered evidence and arguments rather than ignoring them or giving them no weight except in rare circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider evidence presented in a timely manner (Soni; Kao), may not summarily dismiss evidence as insufficient without analysis, should not evaluate rebuttal evidence solely for its 'knockdown' value, and must explain conclusions. The standard is preponderance of the evidence: reject only if, in view of prior art and evidence, it is more likely than not that the claim is unpatentable (MPEP §706; §716.01(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure / public possession requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion of obviousness requires that the reference(s) relied upon, together with the knowledge of a person skilled in the art, be enabling in that it put the public in possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art references (plus ordinary skill) would not have enabled making the claimed compound, that undercuts a prima facie obviousness rejection (In re Hoeksema; In re Le Grice; Ashland Oil v. Delta Resins; In re Grose). Examiners should assess enablement when relying on structural similarity or other prior art teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolation from narrow data / exemplary showings
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results for a single member or a narrow portion of a claimed genus or range may be sufficient to rebut a prima facie case if a skilled artisan could ascertain a trend to reasonably extend the probative value to the claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exemplary showing can suffice (In re Clemens; In re Chupp) but may be insufficient in other circumstances (In re Greenfield; In re Lindner; Grasselli) where different species are not interchangeable or where no adequate basis exists to conclude other claimed compounds would behave similarly. Each case must be evaluated on its totality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success evidentiary specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of commercial success may rebut obviousness but must be supported by hard evidence and be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO lacks means to independently gather such evidence in ex parte prosecution and thus relies on applicant to provide objective proof (sales figures, licensing data). Evidence concerning products not covered by the claims or not commensurate in scope is not probative (Ex parte Remark; In re Huang; GPAC; Paulsen; Kulling). Examiners should evaluate validity of claimed nexus and scope correspondence (Fox Factory; Volvo Penta).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations may be outweighed by strong prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia of nonobviousness, even if present, do not necessarily control the obviousness conclusion if the prima facie case is strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found that strong evidence of obviousness can outweigh secondary considerations (Pfizer v. Apotex; Leapfrog v. Fisher-Price; Newell v. Kenney). Examiners must weigh all evidence, and a mere presence of credible rebuttal evidence does not automatically require withdrawing an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for factual support in declarations and expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Declarations and expert opinions must contain factual support and specifically address the relevant prior art to be probative of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations that only contain conclusory statements or lack facts tied to the specific art are not probative (Beattie). Expert testimony contrary to inventor admissions or prior art disclosures may be rejected (PharmaStem). Ex parte evidence should directly address how it rebuts the Graham factors and the cited references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for determining relevant prior art (AIA vs pre‑AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant time for assessing prior art and obviousness differs depending on whether the application is examined under AIA or pre‑AIA law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For AIA or first-inventor-to-file applications the relevant time is 'before the effective filing date of the claimed invention'; for pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 the relevant time is 'at the time of the invention.' Many cited cases involve pre‑AIA law but principles may apply with appropriate temporal adjustments. See MPEP §2145 and §2150 et seq.
